newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Twelve NZ Maori seats possible as rolls revised.
newsitem.headline: Twelve NZ Maori seats possible as rolls revised.

text.p: The number of Maori electorates would increase to 12 from five if all Maori enrolled on the Maori roll under a so-called electoral option launched on Thursday, according to official statistics.
Under the option, which will run until August 27, those who identify themselves as Maori can register to vote in a separate Maori electorate or a general electorate at the next election, due in 1999.
The total number on the roll will determine how many of the 120 seats in parliament are allocated to Maori voters.
According to Statistics New Zealand, if all Maori enrolled on the separate roll, there would be 12 Maori seats.
At the last election Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters' New Zealand First Party, now the junior partner in the centre-right coalition government, won all five Maori seats.
The number of Maori seats would increase to seven if 17,000 people switched from the general to the Maori roll.
Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare urged Maori to exercise their rights and take part in the option.
"If you have already made your choice, get the message out to other members of your whanau (extended family)," he said in a statement.
Already the number of Maori electorates looks set to increase from the current five to six election, based on February 1997 enrolments and provisional 1996 census information, NZPA reported.
The Maori option was last run by the Government in 1994 and increased the number of Maori electorates from four to five.
However, it also led to High Court action after Maori groups claimed up to 60,000 voters of Maori descent did not get a chance to take part because of an alleged lack of resources and time.
The High Court criticised the government's handling of the option. Maori went to the Privy Council but failed to get last year's election delayed so the option could be rerun.
This year the Government is spending $2.2 million on the option, including a large-scale information campaign.
